title: Key Sites for P2X Receptor Function and Multimerization: Overview of Mutagenesis Studies on a Structural Basis

subsections.section_title: Introduction, Historical Context, and Biological Significance
subsections.subsection_title: Discovery, Nomenclature, and Molecular Identification of P2X Receptors
subsections.content: This review aims to provide a structure-interpreted overview on the mutational analysis of members of the P2X receptor family of trimeric ligand-gated ion channels (tLGIC) ref [1], ref [2], ref [3], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [7], ref [8]. An exciting milestone in the P2X receptor field is the 3-Å resolution of the crystal structure of the zebrafish P2X4 (zfP2X4) receptor in both the unliganded apo-closed state and the ATP-bound open state. These crystal structures provide an invaluable framework to place data that were obtained by probing P2X receptor function through sitedirected mutagenesis and pharmacological interventions into a three-dimensional context. The application of the zfP2X4 crystal structure for the interpretation of mutagenesis data has enormously advanced our understanding of the mechanisms of the molecular operation of the P2X receptor in almost every aspect, including ligand binding, channel gating, pore opening and ion permeation. Based on these and other successful experiences, we feel confident in using the zfP2X4 crystal structures for the visualization of the mutated residues and, whenever reasonable, for the interpretation of the mutagenesis data. In addition to function, emphasis is also placed on the domains and individual residues that are *Address correspondence to this author at the Department of Molecular Pharmacology, Medical Faculty of the RWTH Aachen University, Wendlingweg 2, D-52074 Aachen, Germany; Tel: +49-241-8089131; Fax: +49-241-8082433; E-mail: gschmalzing@ukaachen.de involved in the trimerization of P2X receptor subunits as identified by structure-interpreted mutagenesis studies ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Introduction, Historical Context, and Biological Significance
subsections.subsection_title: Extracellular ATP and the Emergence of P2X Receptors as Signaling Molecules
subsections.content: The first evidence that micromolar concentrations of extracellular ATP exert a neurotransmitter-like action by directly exciting within milliseconds a large conductance in mammalian cells that is permeable to cations, including Ca 2+, and reverses near 0 mV is usually assigned to patch-clamping experiments that were published in 1983 ref [9], ref [10], ref [11]. Molecular cloning has disclosed that all of the P2 receptors with ligandgated ion channel (LGIC) activity belong to the subclass of P2X receptors ref [10], ref [11]. The designation P2X was originally coined to subdivide P2 receptors into two subtypes, P2X and P2Y, based on two broad patterns of potency of ATP analogs as observed in functional assays in isolated organs ref [9], ref [10], ref [11]. This original subdivision into P2X and P2Y receptors from 1985 was found to fortunately fit with the structurally defined subclasses of (ionotropic) LGICs and (metabotropic) G proteincoupled receptors, respectively ref [10], ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Introduction, Historical Context, and Biological Significance
subsections.subsection_title: Structural Basis and Gating Mechanisms of ATP-Gated P2X Channels
subsections.content: P2X receptors play key roles in signal transduction in numerous excitable and non-excitable mammalian cells ref [33, 35, 36]. Growing evidence had implicated P2X receptors in a broad variety of pathological settings, including inflammation, cancer, and neurological disorders, such as neuropathic pain and depression. Accordingly, P2X receptors hold great promise as therapeutic targets for various diseases. No drug that acts on P2X receptors has been approved ref [37, 38]; however, the orally bioavailable P2X3 antagonist AF-219 (a diaminopyridine derivative of undisclosed structure) has successfully completed phase 2 clinical trials for the indications of urinary frequency and chronic idiopathic cough. AF-219 was found, for instance, to dramatically reduce cough frequency and severity in refractory patients ref [38]ref [39]ref [40] and will be further developed for this indication. The clinical development of P2X7 antagonists against rheumatoid arthritis has stopped because of a lack of efficacy ref [41, 42]. However, the P2X7 receptor is independently considered to be a promising target for a number of other diseases, such as pain, Alzheimer disease, major depressive disorder, chronicinflammatory bowel disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease ref [37, 38, 43, 44], and even cancer ref [45]ref [46]ref [47]ref [48]ref [49].

subsections.subsection_title: Biological Roles and Therapeutic Relevance of P2X Receptors
subsections.content: In this chapter, we briefly outline the overall atomicresolution structure of the zfP2X4 receptor and describe the nomenclature of the various protein domains as determined by X-ray crystallography at a 2.8-3.1-Å resolution for both the apo-closed state and the ATP-bound open state of the zfP2X4 receptor ref [22]. No other high-resolution structure of a P2X receptor is presently available ref [22]. The crystal structure of the zfP2X4 receptor verified the homotrimer architecture of this receptor class that was initially revealed by PAGE ap-proaches for virtually all rat or human P2X family members ref [21], ref [22], except for P2X6, which forms aggregates rather than assembling as defined homotrimers ref [22].

subsections.subsection_title: P2X7 Receptor in Cancer and Disease-Related Biology
subsections.content: The definitive confirmation that these intersubunit grooves represent the ATP binding pockets was provided by the crystallization of the zfP2X4 receptor in the ATP-bound open-state. The triphosphate chain and the adenine ring of the ATP molecule adopt a U-shaped configuration within the ATP-binding pocket. The phosphate oxygens of ATP are coordinated by the side chains of K70 zfP2X4 and K72 zfP2X4 of one subunit and N296 zfP2X4, R298 zfP2X4 and K316 zfP2X4 of the adjacent subunit (Fig. 4). In agreement with the labeling of a cysteine mutant of the P2X2 receptor with the thiol-reactive NCS-ATP, hydrophobic interactions with L191 zfP2X4 (see Fig. 5F; corresponding to L186 rP2X2) and I232 zfP2X4 coordinate the adenine base of ATP. The adenine base is further stabilized by hydrogen bonds with the side chain and backbone of T189 zfP2X4 and the backbone of K70 zfP2X4 (Fig. 4). The ribose moiety faces toward the solution and is recognized solely by hydrophobic interactions with L217 zfP2X4. Specific characteristics of the ATP-binding sites at the interface of different subunits as present in heteromeric receptors were recently disclosed by homology modeling.

subsections.section_title: Subunit Assembly, Stoichiometry, and Inter-Subunit Organization
subsections.content:
The ATP concentration dependence of ATP-activated native currents in sensory neurons fitted a model in which ATP must bind to each of three identical, non-interacting sites to open the channel [ref 4]. This finding was most likely the first to suggest that P2X receptors are composed of multiple subunits, akin to other LGICs, such as Cys-loop receptors [ref 12]. The first ATP concentration curve that was published for the cloned rP2X2 receptor showed strong cooperativity with a Hill coefficient of 2.0, also suggesting that more than one ATP molecule must bind before the channel opens [ref 5]. Accordingly, the rP2X2 receptor must either be a monomer that is capable of binding more than one ATP molecule or, more likely given the general oligomeric nature of LGIC, an oligomer having one ATP binding site per monomer [ref 12, ref 20]. Strong evidence for a multimeric nature of P2X receptors comes from the formation of a new receptor phenotype upon the coexpression of recombinant P2X2 and P2X3 subunits. This phenotype includes properties that are akin to both P2X2 and P2X3 receptors by being non-desensitizing and αß-meATP sensitive, respectively [ref 13]. The most plausible explanation is that P2X2 and P2X3 subunits are capable of heteropolymerizing into a heterooligomeric P2X2/3 receptor that faithfully reproduces the receptor phenotype of the native ATPgated channels that are found in sensory neurons [ref 13].

A critical role of the TM2 helix for homo-and heteropolymerization was deduced from the observation that C-terminal truncation at position R304 rP2X2 (corresponding to R312 zfP2X4 or R310 rP2X5, see arrow in Fig. 5A) that also deleted the pre-TM2 region (equivalent to ß strand 14 of the zfP2X4 structure), and the TM2 helix prevented both assembly with full-length P2X2 or P2X3 subunits and selfassembly [ref 2]. This view was further supported by coimmunoprecipitation experiments with two chimeras consisting of the P2X1 ectodomain flanked by the N-and Cterminal domains, including the transmembrane helices of rP2X3 (X3-X1-X3) and vice versa (X1-X3-X1) [ref 2]. The rationale was that wt P2X6 can co-assemble with wt rP2X1 but not with rP2X3 when co-expressed in HEK293 cells [ref 17]. Intriguingly, the X1-X3-X1 chimera co-precipitated with the wt rP2X6 subunit, whereas X3-X1-X3 and wt P2X3 did not [ref 2, ref 17]. This finding was interpreted to support the view that a TM helix harbors a specific recognition motif that is critical for the assembly of P2X subunits [ref 1, ref 2].

Cysteine-scanning mutagenesis of the ectodomain residues E52-G96 hP2X1 combined with comprehensive pharmacological analysis, [ 32 P]2-azido-ATP cross-linking and cysteine modification by thiol-specific reagents identified the residues K68 hP2X1, K70 hP2X1 and F92 hP2X1 as most important for hP2X1 activation and inhibition by agonists and the antagonist suramin, respectively [ref 3, ref 11]. Mapping of the E52 hP2X1 -G96 hP2X1 data together with data from the former cysteine-scanning mutagenesis of flanking regions of the hP2X1 receptor [ref 3] and the in silico molecular docking of ATP and BzATP provided homology models of the ATP-binding site that are consistent with the experimental data [ref 10].

subsections.section_title: Subunit Assembly, Stoichiometry, and Inter-Subunit Organization
subsections.subsection_title: Determinants of Assembly Competence and Trafficking
subsections.content:
Altogether, these findings left no doubt that P2X receptors must be oligomeric proteins similar to the vast majority of ion channels [ref 1, ref 2, ref 3, ref 4]. Additionally, a monomer with just two transmembrane domains appeared unlikely to account for a functional ion channel. Because the lack of homology with known ion channels provided no clue to the possible subunit stoichiometry, the topology with only two membranespanning domains and intracellular N-and C-termini was considered a possible structural hint. Indeed, based on the global membrane topology, P2X receptors appeared structurally more closely related to the inward rectifier K + (Kir) channels, the degenerin/epithelial Na + (DEG/ENac) channels (which also include FMRF amide-gated channels of mollusks and acid-sensing ion channels, ASICs, also designated ACCNs) and the bacterial mechanosensitive channels (mscLs) than to Cys-loop receptors or ionotropic glutamate receptors [ref 6, ref 7, ref 8, ref 10].

The fact that sequence-specific TM2 interactions are not needed to achieve the mature homotrimeric structure does not rule out that interactions between the TM helices play an important role later in the functional life of a P2X receptor as an ATP-gated channel [ref 2, ref 3]. Indeed, there is indirect evidence that the loose packing of the TM helices displayed by the structure of zfP2X4 receptor is defined in part by detergent aggregate known to preferentially occupy the larger volume that surrounds the hydrophobic domain of membrane proteins with large water-soluble domains [ref 10]. Support for this view comes from the observation that the highly tilted and kinked TM helices in the zfP2X4 structure result in a thin hydrophobic thickness (< 20 Å) that is much too short to span a native membrane [ref 10]. The suggestion that the intermonomer fenestrations seen in the structure leave the channel pore open to the fatty acyl environment [ref 10] could be demonstrated by a molecular dynamics simulation of the membrane-embedded zfP2X4 [ref 9]. Relatively modest structural rearrangements of the TM helices were sufficient to improve the hydrophobic mismatch and resulted in the formation of intersubunit interfaces within the membrane by allowing for a much tighter packing of the TM helices [ref 9]. The two following interfaces were identified: (i) TM2 residues L351 rP2X2, I355 rP2X2 and W358 rP2X2 of one subunit interact with L346 rP2X2, A347 rP2X2 and V354 rP2X2 on the adjacent TM2 helix; (ii) TM1 residue Y45 rP2X2 interacts with L340 rP2X2 in TM2 of the adjacent subunit [ref 9].

In a study of the hP2X3 receptor using moleculardynamics simulations and oxidative cross-linking of cys-teines substituted at positions of close proximity between intra-or intersubunit domains, such as the head-domain and dorsal-fin or the dorsal-fin and left-flipper, it was shown that the ATP binding pocket undergoes spontaneous conformational changes even in the absence of ATP [ref 11, ref 13, ref 17]. Interestingly, the spontaneous cross-linking of K201C hP2X3 (dorsal fin) and V274C hP2X3 (left flipper) (Fig. 5H) prevented the binding of ATP to the receptor as analyzed by the fluorescent APT-derivative BODIPY-TR ATP, which was equipotent to αβ-meATP [ref 11, ref 13]. It was concluded that the high conformational flexibility of domains constituting the ATP binding pocket is a prerequisite for agonist binding and receptor activation [ref 11, ref 16, ref 20]. In addition, in the zfP2X4 receptor, ATP recognition is determined by the inherent dynamics of the head domain [ref 11, ref 17]. Inherent dynamics in the absence of ATP and ATP-induced coordinated allosteric changes in the left flipper and dorsal fin domains were also revealed by molecular dynamics and normal-mode analysis of the zfP2X4 receptor and verified by cysteine cross-linking and a engineered zinc bridge between the left flipper and dorsal fin [ref 11, ref 16, ref 19].

subsections.section_title: Subunit Assembly, Stoichiometry, and Inter-Subunit Organization
subsections.content:
The hypothesis that two membrane-spanning helices flanking a differently sized ectodomain represent a general motif that defines the stoichiometry of an oligomeric protein was gradually rejected. The αßγ-ENac was initially been suggested and later confirmed to be organized as a tetramer, but actual data convincingly indicate that αßγ-ENacs are trimers based on quantitative fluorescence analysis and AFM imaging of the ENac itself [ref 7]. The ASICs and P2X receptors are unrelated in amino acid sequence but share significant structural similarities, including the trimeric structure [ref 1, ref 3, ref 4, ref 5].

To identify contact patches that potentially contribute to the assembly of zfP2X4 subunits, we visualized the solventaccessible van der Waals interaction surface according to the hydrophobicity and electrostatic potentials (Fig. 2) [ref 1, ref 10]. By considering the van der Waals surface areas of atoms in a proximity of < 4.5 Å between two adjacent subunits, the subunitsubunit contact surface could be visualized in the closed and open state (Fig. 3) [ref 1]. The specific residues of adjacent subunits that interact electrostatically or via hydrogen bonds or hydrophobic (van der Waals bonds) are listed in Table 1 [ref 1, ref 2]. Fig. ref [2]. Surface-exposed side chains available for zfP2X4 intersubunit interactions. Shown is a representation of surfaceexposed side chains of a single subunit of the zfP2X4 receptor in the apo-closed state (left panel; PDB entry 4DW0 ref [2]) and the ATPbound open state (right panel; PDB entry 4DW1 ref [2]) [ref 1]. Surface areas that are highly prone to protein association and are therefore available for subunit-subunit interactions were determined based on the solvent-accessible Van-der-Waals interactions and colored according to hydrophobicity (green) and negative (red) and positive (blue) electrostatic potential [ref 10]. The electrostatic and hydrophobic potentials were calculated using routines that were implemented in the protein patch analyzer in the MOE2012 [ref 10]. The contact surfaces were identified by calculating the Van-der-Waals surface areas of atoms in a proximity of < 4.5 Å between two adjacent subunits A and B (ribbon colored orange and pink, respectively) [ref 1]. In the middle of the upper and lower panels, the entire zfP2X4 receptor is shown as a ribbon representation (3 rd subunit in gray and with the depiction of the contact surfaces of the orange and pink subunits) [ref 1]. Hydrophilic portions of the contact surfaces are colored gradually pink, while neutral and hydrophobic portions are colored gradually white and green, respectively. The residues that define these domains through interaction with adjacent subunits by means of hydrogen bonds and by hydrophobic and ionic interactions are specified in Table 1 [ref 1, ref 2]. The gray ovals illustrate the extracellular interaction domains I-III of two adjacent subunits A and B (indicated by superscripts): I, head A -to-body B; II, left flipper A -todorsal-fin B; and III, body A -to-body B [ref 2]. The identical numbering is used in Table 1. The graphical representation was generated using MOE2012.10.

An ATP concentration-response analysis of whole-cell currents mediated by the cloned rP2X2 receptor yielded a Hill coefficient of 2.0, suggesting that activation requires the binding of more than one agonist molecule [ref 11]. A similar Hill coefficient of 2.3 for ATP activation was estimated from the ATP concentration dependence of single-channel recordings of rP2X2 receptor-mediated currents [ref 20]. The Hill coefficient is not a reliable indicator of the number of functionally important ligand binding sites. Even in cases of strong positive cooperativity, only a minimum estimate of the number of binding sites that were involved is provided [ref 19]. Therefore, a Hill coefficient of 2.3 indicates that there are at least three ATP binding sites in a functional P2X2 receptor [ref 1, ref 2, ref 3, ref 4, ref 5, ref 12]. Kinetic modeling of the data suggested that the binding sites are not independent and that only fully agonistliganded channels open. Spontaneous openings in the absence of ATP were not observed [ref 20].

subsections.section_title: Subunit Assembly, Stoichiometry, and Inter-Subunit Organization
subsections.content:
Co-immunoprecipitation with monoclonal antibodies (anti-FLAG, anti-HA) in non-ionic detergent (1% Nonidet P-40) was also used to probe for domains that are involved in P2X receptor assembly in HEK293 cells by examining the ability of P2X2 deletion mutants and chimeric constructs to associate with full-length P2X2 and P2X3 subunits in HEK293 cells [ref 1][ref 3]. Neither the N-nor C-terminal intracellular domain (until residue 28 rP2X2 and beyond residue 362 rP2X2, corresponding to 30 zfP2X4 and 370 zfP2X4, respectively) was required for cell surface expression or assembly with the full-length rP2X2 or rP2X3 subunits, as judged by co-immunoprecipitation [ref 1][ref 3]. In addition, the replacement of rP2X2 residues 1-50 (which include the entire TM1 helix) by the cleavable signal peptide of the α7nAChR did not prevent co-immunoprecipitation with the full-length rP2X2 or rP2X3 subunit [ref 1][ref 3]. These data largely ruled out a sequence-specific contribution of the cytoplasmic N-or C-terminal domains or the TM1 helix in subunit recognition [ref 1][ref 3].

The interested reader is referred to several excellent recent reviews on this subject that also contain extensive background information [ref 10][ref 11][ref 9][ref 17][ref 18][ref 20]. One of these review contains a particularly comprehensive and valuable tabular overview about the mutated residues that are involved in ATP binding [ref 10][ref 11].

The hP2X1 receptor mutants K68A hP2X1 and K309A hP2X1, which caused the largest decrease of the ATP potency, did not affect the antagonism by suramin [ref 12][ref 13][ref 14][ref 15]. These and similar results with the mutants of aromatic residues of the hP2X1 receptor raised the question of whether the binding sites for ATP and suramin binding are different [ref 10][ref 12][ref 13][ref 14][ref 15][ref 16].

subsections.subsection_title: Intracellular and Post-translational Modulation of Gating
subsections.content:
The resolution of the ATP-bound open-state structure of the zfP2X4 receptor and its comparison and superimposition to the apo-closed-state zfP2X4 structure revealed the conformational changes underlying the ATP-induced closedto-open transition of the zfP2X4 receptor (channel gating and pore opening) (ref [9], ref [10]). After ATP binding, the intersubunit cleft between the head and the dorsal fin domains closes, and an outward flexing and rotation of the subunits occurs (ref [9], ref [10], ref [12], ref [13]). This flexing results in the substantial expansion of the extracellular vestibule outside of the channel pore, and an iris-like motion of the membrane-spanning helices subsequently occurs that eventually opens the ion channel pore (ref [9], ref [10], ref [12], ref [13]).

Already, early SCAM studies of the rP2X2 receptor addressed the precise localization of the channel gate (ref [12], ref [13]). However, due to the different accessibility of L338 rP2X2, the location of the gate was slightly different in these studies (ref [12], ref [13]). While Rassendren and colleagues reported the gate between L338 rP2X2 and D349 rP2X2, Egan et al. concluded that the gate is located more extracellularly (proximal) of TM2 (between I328 rP2X2 and L334 rP2X2 ) and that TM2 crosses the membrane in a non-helical manner because G342 rP2X2 was accessible by MTSEA + from both sides of the membrane (ref [12], ref [13]). Later, a SCAM study of the rP2X2 receptor using MTSET +, Ag + and Cd 2+ as modification reagents located the gate in the external (helical) half of TM2 between I332 rP2X2 and T341 rP2X2 (ref [12], ref [13]). This study also suggested that TM1 is positioned peripherally to TM2 (ref [12], ref [13]). Considering previous results, the gate region itself may also function as a selectivity filter (ref [12], ref [8], ref [12], ref [13]).

subsections.subsection_title: Extracellular Allosteric Coupling and Intersubunit Gating Interfaces
subsections.content:
Several of the early mutagenesis studies also revealed amino-acid residues involved in the coupling of ATPbinding to channel opening (channel gating). For instance, the T339S rP2X2 mutation that destabilizes the closed state of the receptor and the simultaneous K308A rP2X2 mutation revealed a role in the channel gating of the T339 rP2X2 and K308 rP2X2 residues ref [83]. Later, the T339S rP2X2 mutation of the P2X2 receptor, which has been suggested to alter the equilibrium between the closed-and open-state in favor of the latter, in combination with native (H120 rP2X2 and H213 rP2X2 (Fig. 5J)) ref [77], ref [78], ref [79], ref [82] and engineered Zn 2+ binding sites was instrumental in demonstrating that following ATP binding, the head and dorsal fin domains move closer to each other ref [78], ref [82]. The resulting tightening of the ATP binding sites correlates precisely with channel opening ref [13], ref [30], ref [82]. Thus, the ATP-induced tightening of the ATP binding sites represents an essential early step in the coupling of ATP binding to channel gating and favors the opening of the ion channel ref [13], ref [82]. The competitive antagonist TNP-ATP prevents gating by preventing the tightening of the ATP-binding pocket ref [13].

In the post-crystal structure era, two further SCAM studies using MTS-reagents, Ag + and Cd 2+ ref [80], or only Cd 2+ ref [15] as modification reagents revealed the gates between I332 rP2X2 and T339 rP2X2, and T336 rP2X2 and T339 rP2X2, respectively. The mapping of these residues to P2X2 receptor homology models based on the closed-state crystal structure of the zfP2X4 receptor showed that the narrowest part of the closed-ion conducting pathway is formed by T336 rP2X2 and T339 rP2X2 ref [55] (Fig. 5N), which is in general agreement with the latest SCAM and mutagenesis studies ref [80], ref [81], ref [15], ref [83]. The T339K rP2X2 mutant of the P2X2 receptor was shown to increase anion permeability and reduce unitary conductance gradually when mutated in one, two or three subunits of the P2X2 receptor, indicating that each subunit contributes symmetrically to the open-channel permeation pathway upon the iris-like separation of the three TM2 helices ref [55]. The slight deviations in the accessibility of one or two residues between these studies of the P2X2 receptor can most likely be attributed to the use of cysteine-reactive reagents of different molecular sizes and differences in the experimental setup.

subsections.subsection_title: Transmembrane Gate Rearrangements and Pore Opening
subsections.content:
The need of significant conformational movements at the interface of adjacent subunits during channel gating was previously concluded from disulfide-bond-formation studies between introduced cysteine residues at the extracellular subunit interfaces of several P2X isoforms: the homomeric rP2X1 receptor (K68C rP2X1 and F291CrP2X1 (Fig. 5E)) [ref [93], ref [16]], the heteromeric rat P2X2/3 receptor (V48C rP2X and I328C rP2X2 (Fig. 5K), and V42C rP2X3 and I319C rP2X3 ) [ref [92], ref [93], ref [16]]; and the heteromeric rat P2X1/2 receptor (K68C rP2X1 and F289C rP2X2 ) [ref [93], ref [16]]. Later, a significant movement of the subunit interface at the level of the lower body domain was also found in disulfide trapping experiments of cysteines when introduced in position E63 rP2X2 of one subunit and R274 rP2X2 of the adjacent subunit in the rP2X2 receptor [ref [93], ref [16]]. ATP binding was suggested to induce movements of the adjacent subunits at the level of E63 rP2X2 /R274 rP2X2, resulting in the spatial separation of these residues and a disruption of the putative intersubunit salt bridge between E63 rP2X2 /R274 rP2X2 [ref [93], ref [16]].

Poisson-Boltzmann calculations along with thiol-reactive modifications of introduced cysteine residues in the surrounding of the lateral portals, which were evident from the zfP2X4 receptor structure and homology models of other P2X members, identified the three lateral ion-accesspathways [ref [90], ref [91], ref [93]]. This finding has significantly improved our understanding of how ions access and flow through P2X receptors [ref [91], ref [92], ref [93]]. Interestingly, the fractional and relative Ca 2+ permeability through the ivermectin-sensitive hP2X4 receptor was diminished by ivermectin, which is the first report of an allosteric modulation of the Ca 2+ current of a LGIC by an exogenously applied drug [ref [90], ref [91]]. The E51Q hP2X4 mutation located at the entry of the lateral portals significantly attenuates the effect of ivermectin on the Ca 2+ permeability, indicating a key role of the negative charge at the lateral ion entrance to control Ca 2+ access to the pore [ref [90], ref [91]]. In addition, the permutation of several other residues, such as E56 r/hP2X4, F324 rP2X4, G325 rP2X4, K329 rP2X4, and D331 hP2X4, was shown to affect the permeation properties of the P2X4 lateral portals or central vestibule [ref [90], ref [91], ref [92], ref [19]]. The existing data regarding extracellular access to the transmembrane channel pore were comprehensively reviewed by Samways and colleagues [ref [90], ref [91], ref [92], ref [93], ref [16], ref [19], ref [88], ref [89], ref [84], ref [85], ref [86], ref [87]].

subsections.subsection_title: Access Pathways, Permeation, and Lateral Portal Control
subsections.content:
Two ingenious studies were published that used cis-trans isomerization to engineer a light-gated rP2X2 receptor. One study made use of cysteine substitution mutants of the outer TM helices of the P2X2 receptor, which were previously shown to modify channel gating when chemically modified ref [170]. Attachment of the sulfhydryl reactive maleimide ethylene azobenzene trimethyl ammonium derivative (MEA-TMA), which shows strong photo isomerization from transto-cis-or cis-to-trans-isomers using 365 nm or 525 nm of light, respectively, to V48C rP2X2 or I328C rP2X2 (Fig. 5K), resulted in a P2X2 channel that could be turned on and off by light. The simultaneous mutation of I328C rP2X2 and of K69A rP2X2, which makes the P2X2 receptor ATP insensitive, revealed that the light gating of the channel does not require the natural ligand ATP ref [170]. The expression of the K69A rP2X2 /I328C rP2X2 P2X2 mutant in dissociated hippocampal neurons endogenously expressing the P2X2 receptor enabled the optical control of P2X2-like currents in the absence of ATP that evoked the neuronal activity (action potential firing) of the neurons. These data indicate that this approach will enable the dissection in vivo of the physiological and pathological roles of P2X2 receptors at an unprecedented level of precision by the rapid and reversible control of neuronal activity ref [170].

Based on current whole-cell recordings, heterologously expressed P2X receptors can be divided into rapidly desensitizing (P2X1 and P2X3) and slowly desensitizing (P2X2, P2X4, P2X5, and P2X7) receptors. The time course of desensitization of specific P2X receptors is of significant physiological relevance because desensitization determines the time course of P2X receptor signal transduction.

The modification of the cysteine residues that were introduced into the first transmembrane domain 1 (TM1) by MTS reagents, alanine or tryptophan substitution and the analysis of fractional calcium currents indicated that TM1 residues do not directly contribute to the transmembrane permeation pathway. However, when substituted by cysteine, the residue V48 rP2X2 of the outer TM1 of the P2X2 receptor or the corresponding valine residue of the P2X3 receptor was shown to build an inhibitory cross-link with I328C rP2X2 or I319C rP2X3. This finding led to the conclusion that the valine residue at the outer end of TM1 moves with channel opening.

The functional importance of the 10 conserved cysteines (Fig. 5O) and the disulfide connectivity of each subunit were explored by mutagenesis studies, whereas desensitization itself has been mapped by mutagenesis and chimera studies to multiple extracellular and intracellular regions of P2X receptors including the cysteine-rich head domain, amino terminus, carboxyl terminus, and specific residues in P2X2 and P2X4 receptors (ref [20], ref [104], ref [105], ref [106], ref [108], ref [110]). Disulfide bonds between the conserved cysteine residues were also shown to contribute substantially to the structure of the ligand binding pocket and channel gating, and in P2X1 the cysteine-rich head domain was directly implicated in activation and desensitization (ref [20], ref [104]). Mutagenesis of the intracellular C-terminal cysteine residue C430 rP2X2 revealed that C430 rP2X2 functions as a redox sensor enabling the functional modulation of the rP2X2 channel by the redox state of the cell, consistent with broader evidence that the C-terminal domain contributes importantly to desensitization and recovery from desensitization (ref [105], ref [109], ref [112]). Functional analysis of the wt and mutant human and rat P2X3 receptor revealed that the position of nonconserved C-terminal tyrosine residues controls in part the species-specific properties of the human and rat P2X3 receptors, and a highly conserved tyrosine in P2X3 was further shown to stabilize desensitized states and restrict calcium permeability (ref [114]). A recent study used chimeras between the human P2X1 and P2X2 receptors to assign several properties of these channels to distinct protein domains (ref [109]). It was shown that the agonist potency and efficacy, open-channel properties and recovery from desensitization can be controlled independently by concerted interaction between the intracellular, transmembrane and extracellular domains of the receptor (ref [104], ref [109], ref [110]). For instance, the ectodomain determines the antagonist sensitivity, the C-terminus is involved in recovery from desensitization and the TMs control agonist sensitivity and efficacy, while the N-terminus can regulate agonist efficacy independently of agonist sensitivity (ref [109]). More generally, alternative splicing, intracellular N- and C-terminal determinants, and individual residues have all been shown to regulate desensitization kinetics across P2X receptor subtypes (ref [105], ref [106], ref [107], ref [108], ref [110], ref [111], ref [112], ref [113]).

The discovery of ATP-gated P2X receptors dates back more than 30 years ref [115], ref [116], ref [117], ref [118]. Soon after their isolation by DNA cloning ref [119], ref [120], ref [121], P2X receptors were demonstrated to assemble as trimers ref [122], ref [123], ref [124], which was a new structural motif for a ligand-gated ion channel at that time. Hence, each of the three major classes of ligand-gated ion channels is characterized by its own unique subunit stoichiometry, trimeric for the P2X receptors ref [122], ref [123], tetrameric for ionotropic glutamate receptors ref [125], ref [126] and pentameric for Cys-loop receptors ref [127], ref [128]. Site-directed mutagenesis was instrumental in disclosing key sites of the function and oligomerization of P2X receptor ref [129], ref [130], ref [131]. The event of the high resolution crystal structures of the zfP2X4 receptor in the homotrimeric apo-closed and ATP-bound open states provided and will continue to provide invaluable new insights into receptor mechanisms and subunit assembly ref [132], ref [133]. Beyond doubt, we are in a particularly exciting era of P2X receptor research.
